`Object?`, `dynamic` and `void` are all top types — they hold exactly the same set of values — and they differ only in what the compiler lets you do with one.

### The three tops
- **`Object?`** — the honest one. Anything assigns to it, and you can call only `toString`, `hashCode` and `==` until an `is` check promotes it.
- **`dynamic`** — the same values with static checking switched off. Every member call compiles and is resolved at runtime, so a typo ships as a `NoSuchMethodError`.
- **`void`** — the same values, but the result may not be *read*. `void v = 1;` compiles; `print(v)` is a compile error. That is how a function says "I return nothing you should use".

### The bottom
`Never` is the bottom type: a subtype of every type, and inhabited by no value at all. `final int x = fail('boom');` type-checks when `fail` returns `Never`, because `Never` is an `int` — vacuously.

`Null` is **not** the bottom in null-safe Dart. `null is Object` is `false`; `Null` sits under `Object?` only. Before null safety `Null` was the bottom type, which is why older articles say otherwise.

### The shape of it
`Object` is the top of the non-nullable half of the lattice, and `T?` is shorthand for `T | Null` — so `Object?` is `Object | Null` and covers everything, while `Never?` is just `Null`.

Rule of thumb: `Object?` for a value you will check, `dynamic` only at a decoding boundary you cast away immediately, `void` to forbid using a result, `Never` to say this call does not come back.

Its return type has to be `Never`, not `void` — that is the only thing that tells flow analysis the call does not come back.

Flow analysis walks the function tracking which points are reachable. A call to a `void` function is a statement like any other: control flows past it, so the null check before it buys you nothing and a missing return is still missing. An expression of type `Never` is different — everything after it is marked unreachable, which does four jobs at once:

- The variable you checked stays promoted for the rest of the body
- `body_might_complete_normally` goes away: a `switch` arm ending in `fail(...)` counts as leaving the function
- `Never` is the bottom type, so `final Duration d = fail('...');` type-checks in any context
- The lines after the call are reported as **dead code**, which is a feature — it finds what you forgot to delete

### The async version
An `async` helper has to be `Future<Never>`, and it only ends the flow at the `await`. `if (x == null) failAsync();` leaves the flow alive and the promotion gone, because an un-awaited call is just a `Future`; `await failAsync();` ends it.

### Where it turns up
- `throw` is itself an expression of type `Never`, which is why `value ?? throw StateError('...')` works as an expression
- A `Never`-returning `_unreachable()` in the last arm of a switch over a sealed hierarchy
- `<Never>[]` and `Stream<Never>` — containers whose type argument proves they hold nothing

The mental model: `void` means "returns nothing useful", `Never` means "does not return".

Dart reifies generics: every generic instance carries its type arguments at runtime, so `json['tags']` really is a `List<dynamic>` and the cast to `List<String>` is a genuine type mismatch, not a formality an erased language would have thrown away.

### What reification buys you
- `is` and `as` on generic types answer truthfully — `<int>[1] is List<num>` is `true`, `is List<String>` is `false`
- A type parameter is a real type inside the body, so `if (x is T)` and `x as T` work with no `Class<T>` token and no `inline`/`reified` trick
- A `List<String>` refuses a non-String even when written through a `List<dynamic>` alias, so the container stays honest about itself
- `runtimeType` prints the arguments: `List<String>`, and `Box()` with nothing to infer from prints `Box<dynamic>`

### What it costs
Every instantiation carries a type-argument vector, so `List<String>` and `List<int>` are distinct runtime types rather than one shared erased class — more metadata and less code sharing in AOT. Writes into a covariant generic position are checked on the way in, which is exactly why a wrong element throws instead of quietly corrupting the list.

### The trap
The reified type argument is fixed when the object is **created**, never by the cast. `jsonDecode` builds a `List<dynamic>`, and casting that whole list to `List<String>` fails even though every element is a String. Convert instead: `.cast<String>()` for a checked view over the same list, `List<String>.from(...)` for a real copy you own.

Still out of reach: `T()`. You cannot construct from a type parameter, so pass a factory function.

Dart's generic classes are **covariant** in their type arguments — `List<Dog>` really is a subtype of `List<Animal>` — and that rule is deliberately unsound, so the runtime pays for it with a check on every write.

Kotlin makes you write `out`/`in`; Java makes you write `? extends`. Dart chose ergonomics: no variance annotations, `List<int>` flows into a `List<num>` parameter, `List<Text>` into a `List<Widget>`, and nobody thinks about it. Reading through the widened alias is always safe, because every `Dog` is an `Animal`.

Writing is where it breaks. Generics are reified, so the object is still a `List<Dog>` at runtime and `add` checks its argument on entry:

`TypeError: type 'Cat' is not a subtype of type 'Dog' of 'value'`

### Why this one is nasty
The throw happens at the `add`, inside whatever function was handed the widened list, while the bug is the assignment several layers up. Nothing in the stack trace mentions the line that widened the type, and the analyzer never said a word.

### How to not get bitten
- Take `Iterable<Animal>` in parameters when you only read — it has no `add`, so the whole class of bug becomes unrepresentable
- `List<Animal>.from(dogs)` is a real, writable `List<Animal>`; `dogs.cast<Animal>()` is only a checked view over the same `List<Dog>` and throws on the same `add`
- Return `List.unmodifiable(...)` from a repository if you want read-only enforced rather than merely intended

Rule of thumb: covariance is free while you read, and a runtime bomb the moment you write.

`covariant` tells the compiler to stop enforcing the contravariant-parameter rule statically and to insert a runtime type check at the top of the override instead.

The sound rule is that an override must accept **at least** what the supertype accepts, so `void handle(Animal)` may be overridden by `void handle(Object)` but not by `void handle(Dog)` — a caller holding the supertype could pass a `Cat`. Narrowing is what people actually want, so Dart lets you ask for it: write `covariant` once on the supertype's parameter and every override may narrow, or on the override's own parameter for just that one. A wrong argument then throws:

`TypeError: type 'Cat' is not a subtype of type 'Dog' of 'a'`

Flutter leans on this constantly — `didUpdateWidget(covariant MyWidget old)`, `shouldRepaint(covariant MyPainter old)`, `updateRenderObject`. It is safe there only because the framework hands each element back its own widget type.

### Type parameters are covariant already
`class Cage<T extends Animal> { void put(T a); }` needs no keyword. A member signature that mentions the class's own type parameter is implicitly covariant and already runtime-checked — the same mechanism that makes `List<Dog>.add` throw through a `List<Animal>` alias.

### Why `==` is the exception
`bool operator ==(covariant Money other)` compiles, and it is a bug. `==` is called with arbitrary objects by `List.contains`, `Map` lookups and `Set` membership, so the check fires from deep inside collection code:

`TypeError: type 'String' is not a subtype of type 'Money' of 'other'`

Keep `Object other`, open with `identical(this, other) || other is Money && ...`, and override `hashCode` to match.

The raw bound `T extends Comparable` means `Comparable<dynamic>`, so `compareTo` accepts anything and static checking stops; `T extends Comparable<T>` — an F-bound, where the parameter appears inside its own bound — forces `T` to be a type that can compare to **its own kind**.

With the raw bound, `a.compareTo(b)` type-checks for any `b`, because the parameter is `dynamic`. A mismatch is caught only when the receiver's real `compareTo` rejects the argument at runtime. The F-bound moves that to compile time: `Money` satisfies `T extends Comparable<T>` only if it declares `implements Comparable<Money>`.

### The trap nobody sees coming
`int` does **not** satisfy `T extends Comparable<T>`:

`'int' doesn't conform to the bound 'Comparable<int>' of the type parameter 'T'`

`num implements Comparable<num>`, so `int` is a `Comparable<num>`. Generics are covariant, so `Comparable<int>` is a subtype of `Comparable<num>` and never the reverse. The numeric tower is genuinely not F-bounded, and every generic sorting helper written this way rejects `int` on its first call.

### What to write instead
- For your own value types, `T extends Comparable<T>` is exactly right and documents the intent
- For a helper that must also take `int` and `double`, relax to `T extends Comparable<Object>` — `String`, `DateTime` and `num` all satisfy it, `compareTo` still type-checks, and a genuine mismatch is caught by the covariant parameter check at runtime
- For maximum freedom, take a `Comparator<T>` — `int Function(T, T)` — and let the caller supply the ordering, which is what `List.sort` does

The mental model: an F-bound says "comparable to itself", a plain bound says "comparable to something", raw says "trust me".

On the method, unless the type is part of the object's **state**.

A class type parameter is fixed for the life of the instance and shared by every member, so it belongs there when a field has that type or when two members must agree: `Repository<User>` stores a `List<User>` and returns a `User`. A method type parameter is fresh on every call and solved at the call site, so it belongs there when the type only relates one method's arguments to its own return type. A mapper that decodes anything holds no `T` at all — it should be `T decode<T>(...)`, and then no call site names a class type argument.

### How inference finds it
Dart solves method type parameters in two directions. **Downwards** first: the context type — the variable's annotation, the parameter you are passing into, the enclosing function's return type — flows into the call. **Upwards** second: the actual argument types constrain whatever is left, and the answer is the least type satisfying every constraint.

### The failure mode
If `T` appears **only in the return type**, the arguments constrain nothing, and with no context type inference has zero information — so `T` silently resolves to `dynamic`:

- `final user = decode(body);` — `user` is `dynamic`, and every typo on it compiles
- `final User user = decode(body);` — the annotation flows down and `T` is `User`

Make an argument carry the type instead: a `T Function(Map<String, dynamic>) fromJson` witness pins `T` upwards, so the call site cannot get it wrong even with `var`.

Two more nudges toward the method: a `static` member cannot use its class's type parameter, and a method parameter that shadows the class's `T` is a real source of confusion — name it `R`.

It had nothing to pick from, so it fell back to `dynamic`: a bare `[]` with no context type and no elements infers `List<dynamic>`, and that type argument is reified into the object for good.

Dart runs inference in two directions on every generic call and literal.

1. **Downwards** — the context type flows in first. `List<String> a = [];` makes the literal a `List<String>`, `Set<String> s = {};` makes `{}` a set rather than a map, and passing `[]` into a `List<int>` parameter gives a `List<int>`.
2. **Upwards** — the elements and arguments constrain whatever downwards left open, and the result is the least upper bound of what they see.

Writing `<String>[]` skips both: the type argument is stated, not solved.

### Where upwards inference surprises people
- `[1, 'a']` is `List<Object>`, `[1, 2.0]` is `List<num>`, `[Dog(), Cat()]` is `List<Animal>` — the LUB, not the type you had in mind
- `{}` with no context is `Map<dynamic, dynamic>`, never a `Set`
- A constructor with nothing to go on does the same: `Completer()` is `Completer<dynamic>`, `Box()` is `Box<dynamic>`

### Why `dynamic` hurts more here
`List<dynamic>` accepts every write without a murmur, so the wrong element enters quietly and the failure surfaces at the eventual `as List<String>` — which throws about the *list*, naming neither the element nor the line that added it. A `final` field is the worst case: no annotation, no context, and it lives as long as the object.

The rule: give every empty literal a type, either by annotating the variable or by writing the argument on the literal — `final List<Item> _items = [];` or `final _items = <Item>[];`.

`FutureOr<T>` is an **untagged** union: the value carries no marker saying which arm it came from, so the moment `T` can itself be a future the two arms overlap and nothing at run time can tell them apart. `await` resolves that tie in favour of the future arm and unwraps your data.

It is the only union type Dart has, and it is not a class you could have written. `FutureOr` is hard-coded into the subtype rules — `T <: FutureOr<T>` and `Future<T> <: FutureOr<T>` — which is exactly why both arms go in for free, and why nothing comes back out without a check. It cannot be extended, implemented or imitated, and the language offers no way to declare a second one.

### How narrowing is meant to work
- `if (v is Future<T>)` promotes to `Future<T>` in one branch and to `T` in the other; with exactly two arms, ruling one out leaves the other
- `await v` accepts both and yields a `T`, at the cost of a microtask even on the synchronous arm
- Both work only when the arms are disjoint, which means `T` must be a type that cannot be a future

### Where the type degenerates
- `FutureOr<Object>`, `FutureOr<Object?>` and `FutureOr<dynamic>` carry no information: `FutureOr<Object?>` *is* `Object?`, arms and all
- A generic `FutureOr<T>` in your own class is only safe by convention — Dart has no bound that says "not a future", so a caller may instantiate `T` as `Future<int>` and break narrowing for you
- The one consolation: futures flatten, so a `Future<Future<T>>` cannot actually be built, which is why the loss always lands on the value arm

### What to use instead
A **sealed class** with an exhaustive `switch` is the tagged union Dart 3 gives you: an allocation per value, but each arm is a distinct class, so the ambiguity above cannot occur and the compiler checks that you handled both.

Rule of thumb: `FutureOr` is a calling convention for a concrete `T`, not a container — narrow it at the boundary and store the plain value.

Function types are **contravariant in their parameters** and **covariant in their return type**: a substitute may accept more than the slot promises and return less.

Read it from the call site. Whoever holds a `void Function(Dog)` may call it with any `Dog`, and a `void Function(Object)` survives that call, so it is a legal stand-in. The reverse is not: a slot typed `void Function(Object)` may be called with an `int`, and your dog handler would receive one. The analyzer rejects that assignment outright — there is no `covariant` escape hatch for function types, only for parameters of a method in a class.

### The rules people trip over
- **`void` is a top type**, so any return type is assignable to a `void`-returning slot: `void Function() f = () => 42;` compiles. That is why `onPressed: () => _controller.forward()` is fine even though the body returns a `TickerFuture`.
- **Optional parameters widen the shapes a function fits.** `void ping([int code = 0])` satisfies both `void Function()` and `void Function(int)`; a function with a required parameter fits neither smaller shape.
- **Named parameters**: the substitute must accept every one the slot declares, and may not make required anything the slot left optional.
- **Generic functions instantiate implicitly** from the context type — `int Function(int) f = identity;` selects `identity<int>` for you.

### Where it bites
Callbacks. You write `(Dog d) {...}` for a parameter typed `void Function(Animal)` and the analyzer refuses; widen the parameter and narrow inside with `if (a is Dog)`, or make the widget generic. The same rule applies inside type arguments, so `List<void Function(Object)>` really is a `List<void Function(Dog)>` — variance composes.

Mental model: widen what you take, narrow what you give.

The compiler wrote it for you: assigning a `dynamic` to a typed variable is an **implicit downcast**, compiled into exactly the check `as int` would have produced.

`json['id']` is `dynamic`, so `int id = json['id'];` type-checks statically and defers everything to run time. The two messages differ by a suffix — an explicit cast ends in "in type cast", the implicit one does not — which is the fastest way to tell from a crash report which of the two you are looking at.

### is, as, and the patterns
- `as` converts and throws a `TypeError` on failure. `TypeError` is an `Error`, not an `Exception`: it reports a bug in your code, so catching it around the parsing layer hides the defect instead of handling it.
- `is` never throws. It returns a bool and promotes the operand inside the branch — the right tool at any boundary you do not control.
- Patterns *fail to match* rather than throw, with two exceptions: the **cast pattern** (`final id as int`) and the **null-assert pattern** (`final id!`). Both throw, so `case {'id': final id as int}` blows the switch up instead of falling through to the next case. A type pattern — `case {'id': final int id}` — simply does not match, which is what a parser wants.

### What it costs in release
The checks are compiled into the AOT binary and run in production; no build mode removes them on mobile. A check against a plain class is a class-id test and is nearly free; a check against a generic type (`as List<String>`, `as Map<String, dynamic>`) is a real subtype test served by a runtime cache, so keep it out of hot loops. Two caveats: `--obfuscate` mangles the type names in the message, and on the web `dart2js` does strip exactly the implicit ones (`--omit-implicit-checks`, included from `-O3` up), so data that throws on a phone can produce nonsense in a web release build.

The rule: `is` or a type pattern at the boundary, `as` only where the type is already proven — and turn on `strict-casts` so the implicit ones stop being invisible.

Field promotion is a **library-wide, name-based** property: a private final field is promotable only while no other class in that library declares a non-final field or a getter with the same name.

Since Dart 3.2 a `final` private field promotes like a local, including through another object of the same type. The soundness argument is that nothing outside the library can override it and nothing inside can reassign it. But the analyzer reasons per *name*, not per class — a call site could dispatch to any declaration of `_amount` in the library — so one `int? _amount;` in a neighbouring class disables the promotion in yours. The message names the culprit:

`'_amount' couldn't be promoted because there is a conflicting non-promotable field in class 'Invoice'`

A getter with the same private name does it too, and so does a `late` field. Fields stay unpromotable in all the familiar cases as well: public, non-final, or accessed through an interface.

### The other action at a distance: closures
Creating a function that **assigns** to a local demotes that local right there and for the rest of the body — the closure may run at any time, so the compiler stops trusting the variable from the point the closure exists. Order matters: a check written above the closure literal still promotes, everything below it does not. Reading the variable inside a closure changes nothing.

### What to do
- Rename one of the two members, or make the neighbouring field `final` — the conflict is the whole bug
- Copy the field into a `final` local at the top of the method: a `final` local can never be write-captured or demoted
- Bind with a pattern — `if (_token case final token?)` — which introduces a fresh final variable
- `!` only where you can prove it, remembering it throws when you cannot

Mental model: promotion is a promise that the value cannot change between the check and the use, and the analyzer makes that promise only about something nothing else in the library can write.

At every run-time check, because an extension type is a compile-time view that is **erased to its representation type**: at run time a `UserId` simply *is* a `String`.

The parameter in `extension type UserId(String value)` declares the constructor and the single accessor at once, and `String` is the representation type. There is no wrapper object, no allocation and no indirection — each member call is resolved statically and compiled into a call on the String. The safety is free precisely because none of it survives compilation.

### Where the erasure shows
- `is` and `as` test the representation: `'anything' is UserId` is `true`, `someString as UserId` succeeds, and `case UserId u` in a switch matches every String
- `runtimeType` reports `String`, and `List<UserId>` and `List<String>` are the same reified type, so either casts to the other without complaint
- `==` compares representations, so `UserId('u1') == 'u1'` is `true`
- Members resolve on the **static** type, so calling one through a `dynamic` throws `NoSuchMethodError`
- You cannot declare `toString`, `==` or `hashCode` at all — the analyzer rejects any member sharing a name with an `Object` member

### What the type system does give you
`UserId` is not a subtype of `String`, nor even of `Object` — only of `Object?` — unless you write `implements String`, which exposes the String members and makes it assignable to `String` one way. Without that, passing a raw `String` where a `UserId` is expected is a compile error, and that is the whole benefit: **static** discipline over a primitive at zero run-time cost.

Use it for ids, units and validated primitives that stay inside statically typed code. The moment the distinction has to survive an `is` check, a serialiser or a `Map<Type, …>` lookup, you need a real class.

Because `runtimeType` is the **exact** class of the instance, type arguments included, while every dispatch you actually want is a subtype question — and a `Type` object supports nothing but equality.

The static type is what the analyzer reasons about; `runtimeType` is a reified `Type` attached to the object. Treating one as the other produces both of your misses.

### Why the lookups fail
- Exactness: `Dog().runtimeType == Animal` is `false`, so a registry keyed on `Animal` never sees a `Dog`
- Type arguments are part of the key: `<String>[].runtimeType == List<String>` is `true`, `== List<dynamic>` is `false`
- The class you get may be private and unwritable: `jsonDecode('{"a":1}').runtimeType` is `_Map<String, dynamic>`, and `{}.runtimeType` is `_Map<dynamic, dynamic>`
- Platforms disagree about numbers: `1.0.runtimeType` is `double` on the VM and `int` under dart2js, because the web has one numeric representation

### Testing a type parameter
`case T:` is not a thing — a `case` needs a constant pattern and `T` is a type, not a value. What you can write:
- `if (x is T)` — the check you almost always want. It only *promotes* when the parameter is bounded (`T extends Object`), because an unbounded `T` may be nullable and `Object` is not a subtype of it.
- `T == int` — `Type` identity, so exact again: `T == num` is `false` for `T = int`
- `<T>[] is List<num>` — the trick that asks a genuine subtype question about `T`

For a registry, dispatch on a sealed hierarchy with an exhaustive `switch`, or key on something you own: a string tag in the payload, or a `Type` the caller passes explicitly.

`strict-casts`, and it is the one to enable first: it removes implicit downcasts from `dynamic`, so `String name = json['name'];` stops being legal and is reported as `invalid_assignment` — an error, not a warning.

All three live under `analyzer: language:` in `analysis_options.yaml`. They are language modes rather than lints, so no lint package — `flutter_lints` included — turns them on; `very_good_analysis` does.

### What each one catches
- **strict-casts** — every implicit `dynamic` to `T` assignment, argument and return. That is the JSON boundary, and the reason a "type-safe" codebase still throws `TypeError` in production. Severity: error.
- **strict-raw-types** — a generic type written without arguments where nothing can infer them: `void raw(List items)`, `Future f`. Severity: warning (`strict_raw_type`).
- **strict-inference** — the places where the analyzer had to fall back to `dynamic`: `var x;` with no initialiser, a collection literal with no context type, a generic call nothing constrains. Also a warning.

### Rolling them onto legacy code
1. `strict-casts` first: the best defect-per-fix ratio, and each fix forces a real decision about what the data is — an `as`, a checked read, or a model class
2. `strict-raw-types` next: mechanical, mostly `List` becoming `List<String>`
3. `strict-inference` last; it is the noisiest and largely cosmetic once the first two are done

They apply per package, not per file, so use `analyzer: errors:` to demote a rule to `info` while you burn the list down. Check that CI actually fails on warnings, or the last two will report into an empty room.

Bound every type parameter you intend to dereference, and keep `dynamic` out of every signature; the rest is choosing read-only types on the way in and honest ones on the way out.

An unbounded `T` silently admits nullable types. Instantiate `Cache<String, int?>` and `V? get(K key)` can no longer distinguish "absent" from "stored null", and `if (x is T)` will not even promote — `Object` is not a subtype of a `T` that might be `Null`. Writing `K extends Object, V extends Object` makes both problems unrepresentable and costs a real caller nothing.

### The boundary rules
- **`Object?`, never `dynamic`.** `dynamic` disables checking at every call and spreads: whatever you read off it is `dynamic` again. `Object?` forces the caller to state what they think it is.
- **Ask for the least you need.** An `Iterable<T>` parameter cannot be written through. Returning a `List<T>` you also keep hands out an alias, complete with unsound covariance — return a copy or `List.unmodifiable`.
- **No raw types in signatures.** `List` in a public parameter means `List<dynamic>`, and it makes the call site infectious.
- **Pass factories, not types.** You cannot construct from a `T`, so take a `T Function(Map<String, dynamic>)` instead of asking for a `Type`.

### Never as a sentinel
`Never` is the bottom type, a subtype of everything, which makes it the honest type argument for an arm that cannot occur. `Result<int, Never>` — a result that cannot fail — is assignable to `Result<int, String>`; `const <Never>[]` is a valid empty `List<String>`; `Future<Never>` describes a call that only ever throws.

The test for a generic signature: can a caller instantiate it so that one of your members becomes meaningless? If yes, you are missing a bound.
